name: Reel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds** set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection before ingestion, with Data Protection able to block any ingest that breaches those thresholds. This removes the bottleneck of per-ingest negotiations while keeping risk transparent—Data Protection owns the thresholds, not the model’s internals. Trade-off: we accept that edge cases outside the thresholds won’t be caught until the next model review, but we prioritize speed and clear ownership over perfect coverage.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk in Scope’s pre-approved thresholds is that Data Protection will set them too high to avoid liability, letting risky data slip through—turning the model into a placebo. A better alternative is to require **real-time joint review of flagged ingests** (not just thresholds) with a clear escalation path to leadership when Data Protection blocks. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with Engineering and Data Protection co-monitoring the first 100 flagged ingests.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection** before any ingestion begins, with Data Protection retaining a mandatory override toggle at ingest. This ensures the model’s logic is transparent and defensible while avoiding pipeline slowdowns from per-ingest negotiations. The trade-off is less flexibility in adjusting thresholds dynamically, but it prevents black-box risks and distributes liability fairly. Data Protection and Engineering must sign off on the thresholds upfront—no overrides allowed after ingestion.

name: Sift
text: Pre-approved thresholds still make Data Protection a bottleneck—they turn every ingest into a binary gatekeeper, not a reviewer. Instead, require **Engineering to publish the model’s logic and thresholds in a public repo with Data Protection’s audit stamp**, then let Data Protection pull the plug on *any* ingest they flag—not just the ones the model catches. Settle it by having both teams sign the audit report.

name: Scope
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds** set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection before ingestion, with Data Protection able to override only when scores exceed those thresholds. This removes the bottleneck of per-ingest negotiations while keeping real review power in Data Protection’s hands. The trade-off is less flexibility for rare edge cases, but it forces clear, defensible rules upfront and prevents black-box scoring from slipping through.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk in Scope’s pre-approved thresholds is that Data Protection will see every ingest flagged as "medium" or higher as a rubber stamp—no real review, just compliance theater. A better alternative is to require **Data Protection to review and approve the model’s thresholds quarterly**, not per ingest, while keeping the override toggle for edge cases. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: if thresholds miss real risks, adjust; if not, drop the toggle.

name: Reel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds for automated risk scoring before data ingestion**, combined with a mandatory override by the Data Protection team for any flagged data. This approach maintains efficiency in the ingestion process while ensuring that significant risks are still reviewed. The trade-off is that it may limit the flexibility of the Data Protection team in evaluating risks on a case-by-case basis, but it prevents bottlenecks and maintains the model's transparency.

name: Scriv
text: Pre-approved thresholds shift the black-box problem upstream: Data Protection still can’t audit individual ingests without slowing the pipeline, and Engineering can game the thresholds to avoid scrutiny. The real fix is to require **Data Protection to co-own the model’s training data and logic**—not just approve it—then audit a random 10% of ingests monthly. That distributes liability and ensures real oversight without turning every ingest into a bottleneck.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt **pre-approved model thresholds set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection** before any data ingestion. This removes real-time negotiation, speeds up ingestion, and keeps the model’s logic transparent—no black boxes. The trade-off is less flexibility for edge cases, but it shifts the focus from rubber-stamping scores to enforcing clear, defensible rules upfront. Data Protection and Engineering must co-own the thresholds to distribute liability and ensure alignment.

name: Sift
text: Scriv’s pre-approved thresholds still make Data Protection a bottleneck—they turn every override into a policy debate instead of a real-time safeguard. The better alternative is to let Data Protection adjust thresholds dynamically with a clear audit trail, not pre-approve them. Settle it by testing both: run a 30-day pilot where Data Protection adjusts thresholds in real time, then measure if it slows ingestion more than the pre-approval model.

name: Scope
text: Implement **pre-approved model thresholds** set jointly by Engineering and Data Protection for the automated risk scoring model. This approach ensures that clear criteria are established upfront, streamlining the ingestion process and avoiding bottlenecks while still upholding transparency. The trade-off is that initial setup may take longer as both teams collaborate on the thresholds, but it will result in a more efficient and manageable oversight process moving forward. This balances responsibility and clarity in risk management, preventing the model from becoming a black box.

name: Scriv
text: Pre-approved thresholds shift the black-box problem upstream: Data Protection signs off on rigid rules they can’t explain, while Engineering hides behind "the model said so." The real risk is that we trade one opacity for another—now the thresholds themselves become the unquestionable authority, not the scores. Settle it by requiring Data Protection to document *why* each threshold is defensible, not just what it is.
